Internalizing Chain-of-thought into Looped Transformers

Kehang Zhou    Pinyan Lu ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Computer Science Affiliation: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics Affiliation: kehang.zhou@icloud.com  lu.pinyan@mail.shufe.edu.cn
Abstract

Chain-of-thought (CoT) enables constant-bit-size transformers to perform general-purpose computation through generated tokens (Li and Wang, 2025a), whereas looped transformers carry out the same computation by recurrence in hidden states (latent thought). We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between CoT and latent thought. For a prescribed loop count L=L⁡(n)L=L(n) and a fixed integer k≥1k\geq 1 satisfying s​(n)1/k=Ω⁡(L)s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L), our transformer simulates a time-t⁡(n)t(n), space-s⁡(n)s(n) Turing machine using a context window of O⁡(s⁡(n)/L)O(s(n)/L) and O⁡(t⁡(n)​s​(n)1/k/L)O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}/L) generated tokens, reducing both resources by a factor of LL relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation. The construction also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under the finite-precision kernel specified in this paper.

1 Introduction

Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) can perform general-purpose computation through recurrence. A central notion is Turing completeness: the ability to simulate any Turing machine, the standard mathematical model of algorithmic computation. Informally, a Turing-complete model can carry out any computation that a computer program can perform, given sufficient time and memory.

One form of recurrence is autoregressive generation, in which the model repeatedly appends a token to its sequence and uses the resulting sequence to generate the next token. Chain-of-thought (CoT) uses these generated tokens for intermediate computation (Wei et al., 2022). The context window—the range of token positions accessible to attention—serves as the visible workspace.

Pérez et al. (2021) proved that transformers with autoregressive generation are Turing-complete. The earliest constructions use precision that grows with the input, together with a full-history context that scales with running time (Bhattamishra et al., 2020; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024). The full-history regime has a provable ceiling: with a polynomial-time next-token map and polynomial context, standard full-history CoT decides only languages in 𝖯\mathsf{P}, hence not all of 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE} unless 𝖯=𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{P}=\mathsf{PSPACE} (Yang et al., 2025). Sliding-window attention and summarized CoT then bring the visible context down from the running time to the space bound O⁡(s⁡(n))O(s(n)) (Schuurmans et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Brösamle and Eckstein, 2026), while precision is reduced first to O⁡(log⁡(n+t⁡(n)))O(\log(n+t(n))) and then to a constant (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024; Li et al., 2024). Li and Wang (2025a) complete this line: a constant-bit-size transformer that attends only at fixed relative offsets is Turing-complete. Li and Wang (2025b) then bring the cost down to O⁡(s​(n)1/k)O(s(n)^{1/k}) CoT tokens per simulated machine step by increasing the head–layer product.

Looped transformers provide the complementary form of recurrence, in depth: a shared block is applied repeatedly to the hidden state, performing multiple iterations before emitting a token and carrying intermediate results in latent representations rather than an explicit CoT trace (Giannou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Geiping et al., 2025). This internal reasoning is a form of latent thought (Saunshi et al., 2025; Xu and Sato, 2026), and Saunshi et al. (2025) show that loop iterations can simulate CoT steps one-for-one. How does moving computation from generated tokens into hidden-state recurrence change the context window and the number of generated tokens required for Turing-machine simulation?

Our contribution.

We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between explicit CoT and latent thought. One shared decoder block is applied LL times per generated token, so part of the computation moves from the generated trace into hidden activations. An intermediate queue machine represents the Turing-machine computation, and each of its transitions can be realized either as an explicit CoT step or as one iteration of that block. Relative to the queue-machine simulations of Li and Wang (2025a); Li and Wang (2025b), grouping LL simulated transitions into each generated token reduces both the context window and the CoT length by a factor of LL.

The mechanism is a per-iteration KV cache read through a sliding window. Iteration ll writes its result into the iteration-ll cache, the cached entries together hold the Θ⁡(s⁡(n))\Theta(s(n)) machine cells, and attention at that iteration reads only O⁡(s⁡(n)/L)O(s(n)/L) positions. A context window of that length therefore completes the simulation of an s⁡(n)s(n)-space machine. The learned parameters are fixed, machine-dependent constants: they do not grow with nn or with LL. The positional encoding, the context length, the loop count, and the initial cache are instantiated from the resource bounds. The same construction holds with softmax attention under the finite-precision kernel of Section 5. In the statement below, k′k^{\prime} is the number of tapes of the simulated machine and kk is the hierarchy parameter of the queue simulation (Section 2).

Theorem (informal).

Any (t⁡(n),s⁡(n))(t(n),s(n)) time-space bounded Turing machine can be simulated by a constant-bit-size looped transformer (with its input pre-loaded into the initial KV cache as specified in Section 4.3) with head–layer product K=8​k​k′K=8kk^{\prime} and context window length O⁡(s⁡(n)/L)O(s(n)/L), that takes O⁡(s​(n)1/k/L)O(s(n)^{1/k}/L) CoT steps for each simulated TM step, leading to a total CoT length of O⁡(t⁡(n)⋅s​(n)1/k/L)O(t(n)\cdot s(n)^{1/k}/L), for every loop count L=L⁡(n)L=L(n) and every fixed integer k≥1k\geq 1 with s​(n)1/k=Ω⁡(L)s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L). At L=1L=1, the bounds recover (Li and Wang, 2025b, Thm 1).

For the constructed simulation, explicit and latent reasoning are not two capabilities but two placements of the same general-purpose computation realized by recurrence. Decreasing LL externalizes that computation as generated tokens. Increasing LL folds that many consecutive CoT steps into each token as latent iterations. The loop count is the exchange rate between the external trace and the internal computation.

Proof idea. We fold LL consecutive machine steps of an existing CoT simulation into LL iterations of the shared block, replacing LL generated tokens by one. The obstacle is layer alignment: in ordinary CoT every past token is visible to every attention layer, whereas iteration ll of a looped block reads only iteration-ll cache entries of earlier positions, so the inputs consumed at a simulated step must sit in the cache at the layer that executes it. Li–Wang’s queue-machine simulation admits the required reorganization: each simulated step’s queue fronts are cached at the iteration that consumes them. Section 4.5 shows the alignment on one queue.

Potential messages for real LLMs

The same construction suggests several questions for practical reasoning models. Each is a conjecture: none is backed by an experiment, and none is a claim about a deployed model.

  • •

    Looped transformers have the expressive capacity to internalize a substantial part of a chain of thought into recurrent state. Raising the loop count replaces generated reasoning tokens by computation inside the loop, and general-purpose computation is preserved. The loop count is then a way to separate reasoning computation from the tokens a reader sees.

  • •

    The number of generated CoT tokens need not measure the serial computation a model performs. In the simulation, one generated token summarizes LL consecutive steps, and the intermediate states stay in the recurrent state. Visible length and underlying computation can therefore diverge.

  • •

    At large LL this creates a learning difficulty. The explicit trace is strided: only every LL-th state is emitted as a token, and the steps in between stay latent. Next-token prediction does not supervise those latent steps, so the computation may be difficult to acquire from pretraining alone.

  • •

    The decoupling of explicit reasoning trace and latent computation exposes a potential learning challenge at large LL: the explicit reasoning trace becomes increasingly strided, since only every LL-th computational state is exposed as a token, while intermediate computation remains latent. Such a trajectory is not directly supervised by the standard next-token prediction objective, which conjecturally could make this form of computation difficult to acquire through pretraining alone.

  • •

    The construction also suggests how a long-reasoning model might control latent computation, persistent state, and visible tokens separately: take the loop count as an explicit budget for latent computation, and supervise only selected boundary states, so that not every internal step has to be written out as text.

Section 2 fixes the models of computation, and Section 3 the looped transformer. Section 4 gives the hardmax construction and its main theorem, with the initialization interface stated explicitly (Section 4.3) and a worked example at the end (Section 4.5). Section 5 lifts it to softmax at constant bit-size. Section 6 discusses related work; Appendix A constructs congruent queue lengths, Appendix B records the transformer components, Appendix C the exact softmax kernel contract, and Appendix D the detailed comparison table; Appendix E collects notation.

2 Models of computation

We simulate Turing machines through an intermediate model, a synchronous multi-queue machine, following Li and Wang (2025a); Li and Wang (2025b).

2.1 Turing machines and queue machines

Multi-tape Turing machine.

A k′k^{\prime}-tape Turing machine (TM; k′k^{\prime} is the tape count) is a tuple ⟨Σ,Q,δ⟩\langle\Sigma,Q,\delta\rangle where

  • •

    Σ\Sigma is a finite tape alphabet, including 00, 11, and a blank symbol #\#.

  • •

    QQ is a finite set of states, including a start state qstartq_{\mathrm{start}} and halting states qacc,qrejq_{\mathrm{acc}},q_{\mathrm{rej}}.

  • •

    δ:Q×Σk′→Q×Σk′−1×({Left,Stay,Right})k′\delta:Q\times\Sigma^{k^{\prime}}\to Q\times\Sigma^{k^{\prime}-1}\times(\{\mathrm{Left},\mathrm{Stay},\mathrm{Right}\})^{k^{\prime}} is a transition function.

The first tape is a read-only input tape, initially holding a finite {0,1}\{0,1\}-string of input xx; the remaining k′−1k^{\prime}{-}1 tapes start empty. A TM is (t⁡(n),s⁡(n))(t(n),s(n)) time-space bounded if, on every input of length nn, it halts within t⁡(n)t(n) steps and visits at most s⁡(n)s(n) distinct cells across the k′k^{\prime} tapes. Throughout the paper, k′k^{\prime} always denotes the tape count, leaving kk free for the hierarchy exponent of Fact 2.2 below.

Synchronous multi-queue machine.

The intermediate model is a synchronous multi-queue machine: the multi-queue form of the Post machine (Post, 1936) in the variant of Li and Wang (2025b, §2.2). Each queue is a first-in, first-out tape, read at the front and written at the rear. At every step every queue pops its front symbol and appends one symbol, so the queues move in lockstep. There is no separate stay-or-move choice; every front advances by one cell.

  • •

    Σ\Sigma is a finite alphabet, containing 00, 11, and the blank #\#.

  • •

    QQ is a finite state set, containing the start state qstartq_{\mathrm{start}} and the halting states qacc,qrejq_{\mathrm{acc}},q_{\mathrm{rej}}.

  • •

    δ:Q×ΣK→Q×ΣK\delta:Q\times\Sigma^{K}\to Q\times\Sigma^{K} reads the KK front symbols and returns the next state together with the KK symbols appended at the rears.

Initially the input queue holds the input string and the other K−1K{-}1 queues hold only blanks. The space of a queue machine is the maximum number of symbols stored in its queues during the computation, over inputs of length nn. In the rest of the paper, s⁡(n)s(n) is only the simulated Turing machine’s space bound; the queue machine uses O⁡(s⁡(n))O(s(n)) space.

We take queue 00 to be the input queue, and it is the longest. Every halting state is absorbing: for q∈{qacc,qrej}q\in\{q_{\mathrm{acc}},q_{\mathrm{rej}}\} and every KK-tuple σ∈ΣK\sigma\in\Sigma^{K}, set δ⁡(q,σ)=(q,#,…,#)\delta(q,\sigma)=(q,\#,\dots,\#). The convention makes every run an infinite log. It adds at most L−1L{-}1 extra transitions in the final pass; the halting verdict is unchanged (Proposition 4.2).

Definition 2.1 (K-queue execution log).

Let M=(Σ,Q,δ)M=(\Sigma,Q,\delta) be a synchronous KK-queue machine with fixed queue lengths ℓ0,…,ℓK−1\ell_{0},\dots,\ell_{K-1}, on input x=x0⋯xn−1x=x_{0}\cdots x_{n-1} of length n≤ℓ0n\leq\ell_{0}, and let smax=maxr⁡ℓrs_{\max}=\max_{r}\ell_{r}. Its execution log is (σm,qm)m≥0(\sigma_{m},q_{m})_{m\geq 0}, where σm=(σm(0),…,σm(K−1))\sigma_{m}=(\sigma^{(0)}_{m},\dots,\sigma^{(K-1)}_{m}). The entries with m≤smax−1m\leq s_{\max}-1 are given directly: the input feed, for 0≤m≤n−10\leq m\leq n-1,

(σm,qm)=(xm,#K−1,qstart),(\sigma_{m},\,q_{m})=(x_{m},\ \#^{K-1},\ q_{\mathrm{start}}),

and the padding, for n≤m≤smax−1n\leq m\leq s_{\max}-1,

(σm,qm)=(#K,qstart).(\sigma_{m},\,q_{m})=(\#^{K},\ q_{\mathrm{start}}).

For m≥smax−1m\geq s_{\max}-1,

(qm+1,σm+1)=δ⁡(qm,σm−ℓ0+1(0),…,σm−ℓK−1+1(K−1)),(q_{m+1},\,\sigma_{m+1})=\delta\big(q_{m},\ \sigma^{(0)}_{m-\ell_{0}+1},\ \dots,\ \sigma^{(K-1)}_{m-\ell_{K-1}+1}\big),

every front index m−ℓr+1≥smax−ℓr≥0m-\ell_{r}+1\geq s_{\max}-\ell_{r}\geq 0 being given or previously produced; the absorbing convention makes the log infinite. The remaining run length after the cache is filled is

τ⁡(n)=max⁡(1,min⁡{m∣qm∈{qacc,qrej}}−(smax−1)).\tau(n)=\max\big(1,\ \min\{m\mid q_{m}\in\{q_{\mathrm{acc}},q_{\mathrm{rej}}\}\}-(s_{\max}-1)\big).

The step-mm front of queue rr is the symbol appended at step m−ℓr+1m-\ell_{r}+1; τ⁡(n)\tau(n) counts the transitions from step smax−1s_{\max}-1, the first step whose fronts are available, to the first halting state.

The conversion from Turing machines to this model is cited, not re-derived:

Fact 2.2 (Queue Turing machines are Turing-complete (Li and Wang, 2025b, Thm. 2, Step I)).

For every fixed integer k≥1k\geq 1, a t⁡(n)t(n)-time, s⁡(n)s(n)-space k′k^{\prime}-tape Turing machine converts to a synchronous K=6​k​k′K=6kk^{\prime}-queue machine running in O⁡(t⁡(n)​s​(n)1/k)O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}) steps and O⁡(k′​s​(n))O(k^{\prime}s(n)) total queue space. Each tape becomes two stacks and each stack kk levels of queues. Writing B=⌈s​(n)1/k⌉B=\lceil s(n)^{1/k}\rceil, level gg (1≤g≤k1\leq g\leq k) uses two content-half queues of length BgB^{g} and one buffer of length 2​Bg2B^{g}; consecutive half lengths divide one another, and the cost analysis is in terms of these lengths (Li and Wang, 2025b, §3).

Two remarks on scope. First, the level structure and the cost bounds are what we cite; the congruent base bb, the single length per level, the buffer split, and the resource bookkeeping are argued in Appendix A. Second, kk is fixed before instantiation (it sets the head count K=8​k​k′K=8kk^{\prime}) and LL is prescribed afterwards, subject to s​(n)1/k=Ω⁡(L)s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L).

3 The model: looped transformers with a per-iteration cache

3.1 Decoder-only transformers with sliding-window attention

A decoder-only transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) is a parameterized next-token map 𝒱∗→𝒱\mathcal{V}^{*}\to\mathcal{V}. The forward pass for position ii sets hi(0)=emb⁡(vi)h_{i}^{(0)}=\mathrm{emb}(v_{i}) and applies, at each layer ll, an attention sublayer followed by a feed-forward network, both with residual connections:

hi(l+0.5)=WO(l)⋅concath(∑js(l)h,i,j⋅Wv(l,h)hj(l)),h~i(l)=hi(l+0.5)+b(l)+hi(l),hi(l+1)=FF(l)​(h~i(l))+h~i(l),\begin{multlined}h_{i}^{(l+0.5)}=W_{O}^{(l)}\cdot\mathrm{concat}_{h}\Big(\sum_{j}s^{(l)}_{h,i,j}\cdot W_{v}^{(l,h)}\,h_{j}^{(l)}\Big),\qquad\tilde{h}_{i}^{(l)}=h_{i}^{(l+0.5)}+b^{(l)}+h_{i}^{(l)},\\ h_{i}^{(l+1)}=\mathrm{FF}^{(l)}\big(\tilde{h}_{i}^{(l)}\big)+\tilde{h}_{i}^{(l)},\end{multlined}

where the inner sums range over the context window and the concatenation runs over the HH heads. The learned parameters comprise the embedding and output head, query and key matrices Wq(l,h),Wk(l,h)∈ℝdk×dW_{q}^{(l,h)},W_{k}^{(l,h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d}, value matrices Wv(l,h)∈ℝdv×dW_{v}^{(l,h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d}, output matrices WO(l)∈ℝd×H​dvW_{O}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times Hd_{v}}, biases b(l)b^{(l)}, and feed-forward networks FF(l)\mathrm{FF}^{(l)}. A relative positional function pos(l):ℕ→ℝdk\mathrm{pos}^{(l)}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} is specified separately and enters the key side of the scores: the weights sh,i,⋅(l)s^{(l)}_{h,i,\cdot} form the hardmax distribution (all weight on the score’s maximizer) over scores ⟨Wq(l,h)​hi(l),Wk(l,h)​hj(l)+pos(l)​(i−j)⟩\langle W_{q}^{(l,h)}h_{i}^{(l)},\,W_{k}^{(l,h)}h_{j}^{(l)}+\mathrm{pos}^{(l)}(i-j)\rangle. The next token is vi+1=argmax⁡(Wout​hi(L))v_{i+1}=\mathrm{argmax}(W_{\mathrm{out}}h_{i}^{(L)}) at the last layer, for a decoder of depth LL.

In the sliding-window setting with window ww, position ii attends to {i−w+1,…,i}∩ℕ\{i-w+1,\ldots,i\}\cap\mathbb{N}. The KV cache is indexed by (position, layer): Wk(l,h)​hj(l)W_{k}^{(l,h)}h_{j}^{(l)} and Wv(l,h)​hj(l)W_{v}^{(l,h)}h_{j}^{(l)} are written and fixed when position jj completes layer ll.

Remark.

With sliding-window attention and a persistent KV cache, a layer-LL transformer can depend on L⁡(w−1)+1L(w-1)+1 positions, more than the visible window. This span alone does not provide the alignment needed for simulation: each queue value must still sit in the correct iteration’s cache (Section 4.5).

3.2 Looped transformers

Looped transformers re-apply a fixed unit instead of stacking independently parameterized layers (Giannou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Geiping et al., 2025). We adopt a weight-tying version (Dehghani et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2020): the unit acts LL times on the current position’s residual stream per generated token, with a separate per-iteration KV cache carrying state across positions.

Definition 3.1 (looped transformer).

A looped transformer is a decoder-only transformer consisting of

  • •

    a loop unit uφu_{\varphi}: a stack of p≥1p\geq 1 decoder layers specified by the shared weights φ\varphi;

  • •

    the embedding emb\mathrm{emb} and the output head WoutW_{\mathrm{out}}, applied outside the loop;

together with a loop count L∈ℕL\in\mathbb{N}. Given LL, the forward pass computes

hi(0)\displaystyle h_{i}^{(0)} =emb(vi),hi(l+1)=uφ(hi(l);𝒞i(l))(0≤l<L),\displaystyle=\mathrm{emb}(v_{i}),\qquad h_{i}^{(l+1)}=u_{\varphi}\big(h_{i}^{(l)};\,\mathcal{C}_{i}^{(l)}\big)\quad(0\leq l<L),
vi+1\displaystyle v_{i+1} =argmax⁡(Wout​hi(L)),\displaystyle=\mathrm{argmax}\big(W_{\mathrm{out}}\,h_{i}^{(L)}\big),

the ll-th application of uφu_{\varphi} being iteration ll (layer and iteration are used interchangeably). Unrolling the loop yields a p​LpL-layer transformer in which each iteration applies the same pp layers. Shared parameters are independent of LL.

Reading rule (per-iteration cache).

The cache 𝒞i(l)\mathcal{C}_{i}^{(l)} holds the iteration-ll key and value entries of the retained positions j<ij<i. Iteration ll of position ii attends only to those same-iteration entries; the current position’s key and value are computed from hi(l)h_{i}^{(l)} and are frozen when written. A fixed iteration never reads another iteration’s cache. Section 4.5 shows the discipline on one queue, and the construction has to follow it.

A looped transformer is constant-bit-size if the number of distinct learned parameters, their bit precision, and the bit precision of scalar intermediate values are all O⁡(1)O(1), independently of input length, loop count, and generation length.

4 The hardmax construction

We first construct the simulation with hardmax attention; Section 5 realizes the same selection exactly under a finite-precision softmax kernel. Throughout this section, queue rr has length ℓr≡1(modL)\ell_{r}\equiv 1\pmod{L} (queue lengths satisfying this congruence are constructed in Appendix A). Set w=maxr⁡wrw=\max_{r}w_{r} and smax=maxr⁡ℓrs_{\max}=\max_{r}\ell_{r}. Each forward pass executes LL consecutive machine steps. Head rr reads the front of queue rr at distance wr−1w_{r}-1: attention retrieves that front by a fixed relative offset, and the feed-forward network applies the transition.

4.1 Tokens and residual layout

At nonterminal position ii, the token is (qL​i,σL​i)(q_{Li},\sigma_{Li}), where σL​i=(σL​i(0),…,σL​i(K−1))∈ΣK\sigma_{Li}=(\sigma^{(0)}_{Li},\dots,\sigma^{(K-1)}_{Li})\in\Sigma^{K} is the tuple appended at log index L​iLi. Generated tokens are thus machine-state symbols, not natural-language steps.

The embedding uses the layout specified in Appendix B:

hi(0)=(1,eqL​i,onehot⁡(σL​i(0)),…,onehot⁡(σL​i(K−1)), 0|Σ|​K).h_{i}^{(0)}=\bigl(1,\ e_{q_{Li}},\ \mathrm{onehot}(\sigma^{(0)}_{Li}),\dots,\mathrm{onehot}(\sigma^{(K-1)}_{Li}),\ 0^{|\Sigma|K}\bigr).

The blocks store respectively a constant, the current state, the appended tuple, and KK scratch registers for retrieved fronts, giving d=2​|Σ|​K+|Q|+1=Θ⁡(K)d=2|\Sigma|K+|Q|+1=\Theta(K). At iteration ll, attention writes the fronts and the feed-forward network applies δ\delta, leaving the residual equal to the embedding of (qL​i+l+1,σL​i+l+1)(q_{Li+l+1},\sigma_{Li+l+1}). After iteration L−1L-1, the output head emits (qL⁡(i+1),σL⁡(i+1))(q_{L(i+1)},\sigma_{L(i+1)}), or ACCEPT/REJECT if the state is halting, and the generation stops.

4.2 Positional encoding and the attention heads

The relative positional encoding is the simplified form of Li and Wang (2025b, Eq. (2)): writing ere_{r} for the basis vector of ℝdk\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} indexed by head number rr (Appendix B fixes the indexing conventions), dk=Kd_{k}=K,

pos(i−j)=Δ∑r:i−j=wr−1er,\mathrm{pos}(i-j)\;=\;\Delta\!\!\sum_{r:\,i-j=w_{r}-1}\!\!e_{r},

whose rr-th coordinate is Δ\Delta exactly at distance i−j=wr−1i-j=w_{r}-1. The query of head rr is the constant ere_{r} and the key is set to be 00. The positional encoding enters the key side of the scores (Section 3). Thus

scorer(i,j)=⟨er,pos(i−j)⟩=Δ[i−j=wr−1].\mathrm{score}_{r}(i,j)=\left\langle e_{r},\ \mathrm{pos}(i-j)\right\rangle=\Delta[\,i-j=w_{r}-1\,].

For every pass i≥w−1i\geq w-1, j∗=i−wr+1j^{*}=i-w_{r}+1 is the unique maximizer, so hardmax selects queue rr’s designated position: the offset wr−1w_{r}-1 encodes “front of queue rr at the current iteration,” and Lemma 4.1 proves that the entry selected is the front consumed at step L​i+lLi+l. Equal-length queues remain separate via distinct heads and value projections. Appendix B gives the matrices.

Value entries and transition.

Let Vr​(j,l)=Wv(r)​hj(l)∈ℝdvV_{r}(j,l)=W_{v}^{(r)}h_{j}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}, dv=|Σ|d_{v}=|\Sigma|, be head rr’s cached value at position jj and iteration ll, and let V⁡(j,l)V(j,l) denote the represented KK-tuple. Each Wv(r)W_{v}^{(r)} projects symbol block rr; WOW_{O} writes the selected values into the front blocks, and the feed-forward network applies δ\delta. All LL iterations share the same positional encoding, value projections, and δ\delta lookup, so the construction satisfies Definition 3.1.

4.3 The loop invariant

Initialization.

Generation begins at pass w−1w-1 with a loaded cache: for 0≤i≤w−20\leq i\leq w-2 and 0≤l≤L−10\leq l\leq L-1, set the cached value entry V⁡(i,l)=σL​i+lV(i,l)=\sigma_{Li+l}, and set the current token to (qL⁡(w−1),σL⁡(w−1))(q_{L(w-1)},\sigma_{L(w-1)}). Since L⁡(w−1)=smax−1L(w-1)=s_{\max}-1, the first simulated transition occurs at step smax−1s_{\max}-1; the remaining run length is τ⁡(n)\tau(n) (Definition 2.1).

We treat this initialization as an explicit interface assumption. It prescribes which entries a working system must place in the cache before generation; the cost of producing them is not included in any bound of this paper, and we do not prove that a natural-order prompt prefill computes them.

Lemma 4.1.

For every position ii and iteration ll, the value entry V⁡(i,l)V(i,l) encodes the KK-tuple at log index L​i+lLi+l: block rr holds σL​i+l(r)\sigma^{(r)}_{Li+l}.

Proof.

The initialization gives the claim for 0≤i≤w−20\leq i\leq w-2 and all ll, and the token at position w−1w-1 supplies its iteration-00 entry V⁡(w−1,0)=σL⁡(w−1)V(w-1,0)=\sigma_{L(w-1)}.

Consider pass i≥w−1i\geq w-1 and iteration ll, and suppose the residual entering iteration ll contains (qL​i+l,σL​i+l)(q_{Li+l},\sigma_{Li+l}). Head rr attends to position i−wr+1i-w_{r}+1, whose iteration-ll entry was written in an earlier pass and is therefore the log entry

V​(i−wr+1,l)(r)=σL⁡(i−wr+1)+l(r)=σL​i+l−ℓr+1(r),V(i-w_{r}{+}1,\,l)^{(r)}\;=\;\sigma^{(r)}_{L(i-w_{r}+1)+l}\;=\;\sigma^{(r)}_{Li+l-\ell_{r}+1},

the front of queue rr for step L​i+lLi+l, because ℓr−1=L⁡(wr−1)\ell_{r}-1=L(w_{r}-1). The residual stream supplies qL​i+lq_{Li+l}, and the feed-forward network computes

(qL​i+l+1,σL​i+l+1)=δ⁡(qL​i+l,σL​i+l−ℓ0+1(0),…,σL​i+l−ℓK−1+1(K−1)).(q_{Li+l+1},\ \sigma_{Li+l+1})\;=\;\delta\big(q_{Li+l},\ \sigma^{(0)}_{Li+l-\ell_{0}+1},\dots,\sigma^{(K-1)}_{Li+l-\ell_{K-1}+1}\big).

For l<L−1l<L-1, this result is cached as V⁡(i,l+1)V(i,l+1), and the residual entering iteration l+1l+1 contains (qL​i+l+1,σL​i+l+1)(q_{Li+l+1},\sigma_{Li+l+1}); for l=L−1l=L-1, the output head emits (qL⁡(i+1),σL⁡(i+1))(q_{L(i+1)},\sigma_{L(i+1)}), whose embedding supplies V⁡(i+1,0)V(i+1,0). Every value entry is therefore the corresponding log entry, as claimed. ∎

Figure 1 illustrates one pass.

4.4 The main theorem

Proposition 4.2 (queue-level construction).

Let M=(Σ,Q,δ)M=(\Sigma,Q,\delta) be a synchronous KK-queue machine over a fixed alphabet Σ\Sigma, with absorbing halting states and lengths ℓr=L⁡(wr−1)+1\ell_{r}=L(w_{r}-1)+1. Under the initialization of Section 4.3, the construction of Sections 4.1–4.3 gives a decoder-only looped transformer with one shared block, KK heads, window w=maxr⁡wrw=\max_{r}w_{r}, embedding dimension 2​|Σ|​K+|Q|+12|\Sigma|K+|Q|+1, and constant bit-size. It emits the execution log at stride LL and therefore uses

Tcot=⌈τ⁡(n)L⌉T_{\mathrm{cot}}=\left\lceil\frac{\tau(n)}{L}\right\rceil

generated tokens, including at most L−1L-1 absorbing transitions in the final pass.

Proof.

The decoder block, KK heads, window ww, dimension 2​|Σ|​K+|Q|+12|\Sigma|K+|Q|+1, and constant bit-size are those of Sections 4.1–4.2. By Lemma 4.1, at every pass i≥w−1i\geq w-1 and every iteration ll the cached values are the log entries σL​i+l\sigma_{Li+l}, so head rr retrieves the front of queue rr at machine step L​i+lLi+l and the feed-forward network applies δ\delta. After LL iterations the residual is therefore the embedding of (qL⁡(i+1),σL⁡(i+1))(q_{L(i+1)},\sigma_{L(i+1)}). Appendix B (B.6) emits this pair as the token at position i+1i+1, or ACCEPT/REJECT if the state is halting. Generation thus starts from the initialization of Section 4.3 at index L⁡(w−1)=smax−1L(w-1)=s_{\max}-1 and follows the log at stride LL for the remaining τ⁡(n)\tau(n) steps, giving Tcot=⌈τ⁡(n)/L⌉T_{\mathrm{cot}}=\lceil\tau(n)/L\rceil with at most L−1L-1 absorbing transitions in the final pass. ∎

Theorem 4.3.

Any (t⁡(n),s⁡(n))(t(n),s(n)) time-space bounded k′k^{\prime}-tape Turing machine can be simulated by a constant-bit-size looped transformer (with its input encoded in the initial KV cache as specified in Section 4.3) with head–layer product K=8​k​k′K=8kk^{\prime} and context window length O⁡(s⁡(n)/L)O(s(n)/L), that takes O⁡(s​(n)1/k/L)O(s(n)^{1/k}/L) CoT steps for each simulated TM step, leading to a total CoT length of O⁡(t⁡(n)⋅s​(n)1/k/L)O(t(n)\cdot s(n)^{1/k}/L), for every loop count L=L⁡(n)L=L(n) and every fixed integer k≥1k\geq 1 with s​(n)1/k=Ω⁡(L)s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L).

Proof.

For the prescribed LL and the given fixed kk satisfying s​(n)1/k=Ω⁡(L)s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L), the congruent lengths supplied by Appendix A (Lemma A.1) give a step-equivalent K=8​k​k′K=8kk^{\prime}-queue simulation with run length τ⁡(n)=O⁡(t⁡(n)​s​(n)1/k)\tau(n)=O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}) and window w=O⁡(s⁡(n)/L)w=O(s(n)/L). Proposition 4.2 yields

Tcot=O⁡(t⁡(n)​s​(n)1/kL).T_{\mathrm{cot}}=O\!\left(\frac{t(n)s(n)^{1/k}}{L}\right).

Multiplying by LL gives the serial-work bound. The cache stores ww positions at each of LL iterations, so total KV state is Θ⁡(L​w)=Θ⁡(s⁡(n))\Theta(Lw)=\Theta(s(n)). ∎

Resource accounting.

The factor-LL reduction applies to visible resources only: generated tokens and the visible window shrink by LL, while the total cached KV state Θ⁡(L​w)=Θ⁡(s⁡(n))\Theta(Lw)=\Theta(s(n)) and the serial block work L⋅Tcot=O⁡(t⁡(n)​s​(n)1/k)L\cdot T_{\mathrm{cot}}=O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}) are unchanged from L=1L=1. Table 1 tabulates both regimes. The KK heads of the single shared block are re-applied at each iteration, so the head–layer product does not grow with LL.

A concrete instance: the balanced point s⁡(n)=m2s(n)=m^{2}, k=2k=2, L=Θ⁡(m)L=\Theta(m) is admissible because s​(n)1/k=m=Ω⁡(L)s(n)^{1/k}=m=\Omega(L), and it gives O⁡(t⁡(n))O(t(n)) generated tokens, a window of O⁡(m)O(m) positions, Θ⁡(m2)\Theta(m^{2}) cached entries, and O⁡(t⁡(n)​m)O(t(n)m) loop executions.

4.5 A worked example

Take one queue of length ℓ=7\ell=7 and loop count L=3L=3. The window is then w=3w=3: at pass ii and iteration ll, the head reads position i−2i-2, at relative distance w−1=2w-1=2, in the same iteration. Since ℓ−1=6=L⁡(w−1)\ell-1=6=L(w-1), the entry at position i−2i-2 and iteration ll is the front consumed at step 3​i+l3i+l. The construction keeps a separate copy of this bookkeeping for every queue. One queue is enough to see the alignment.

Before generation, the loaded cache of Section 4.3 must already hold V⁡(i,l)=σL​i+lV(i,l)=\sigma_{Li+l} for 0≤i≤w−2=10\leq i\leq w-2=1 and l∈{0,1,2}l\in\{0,1,2\}: σ0,σ1,σ2\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2} at position 00 and σ3,σ4,σ5\sigma_{3},\sigma_{4},\sigma_{5} at position 11, together with the token (q6,σ6)(q_{6},\sigma_{6}) at position 22. Here L⁡(w−1)=6=smax−1L(w-1)=6=s_{\max}-1, and smax=7s_{\max}=7 is the length of this queue, so generation begins at step 66, the first step whose front is already in the cache.

Table 2 lists the first passes. At pass i=3i=3 the three iterations execute steps 99, 1010, and 1111, and iteration ll reads V⁡(1,l)=σ3+lV(1,l)=\sigma_{3+l}. On a queue of length 77, the symbol consumed at step mm was appended at step m−7+1m-7+1, so those fronts are the symbols appended at steps 33, 44, and 55. In general, the symbol read at pass ii and iteration ll has log index

3​(i−2)+l= 3​i+l−7+1.3(i-2)+l\;=\;3i+l-7+1.

Each pass advances the machine from log index 3​i3i to 3​i+33i+3 and emits the state at the boundary. The visible tokens (q6,σ6),(q9,σ9),(q12,σ12),…(q_{6},\sigma_{6}),(q_{9},\sigma_{9}),(q_{12},\sigma_{12}),\dots are the log sampled at stride L=3L=3. Intermediate steps, such as steps 77 and 88 inside pass 22, are never emitted.

Three features of the example are what the construction uses. First, iteration 11 of pass 33 reads V⁡(1,1)=σ4V(1,1)=\sigma_{4}: the same iteration of an earlier position. It does not read an iteration-00 entry, and it does not mix iterations. Section 3 states this per-iteration rule. Second, a value entry is frozen once written. Initialization supplies V⁡(1,⋅)V(1,\cdot); pass 22 writes V⁡(2,⋅)V(2,\cdot), and pass 44 reads that same entry. Third, the window has to be the one the congruence gives. The front required at step 1111 is σ5\sigma_{5}, written at position 11, exactly w−1=2w-1=2 positions back. With a window of 22, position 11 would already lie outside the positions pass 33 can read. We call a representation layer-aligned when, at every simulated step, the inputs that step consumes already sit in the KV cache at the iteration, or layer, that executes the step.

5 Softmax simulates hardmax at constant bit-size

Section 4 uses hardmax attention. Theorem 4.3 also holds for a max-first binary32 softmax kernel, with no growth in precision as the window or the loop count grows. The five-clause kernel contract, the underflow arithmetic, and the complete proof are in Appendix C.

Write ai,ja_{i,j} for the attention score of candidate position jj in the row of query position ii. For a row with unique maximizer j∗j^{*}, define the attention score gap

Δ=ai,j∗−maxj≠j∗⁡ai,j,\Delta\;=\;a_{i,j^{*}}\;-\;\max_{j\neq j^{*}}a_{i,j},

the score separation of (Brösamle and Eckstein, 2026, Def. D.1).

The kernel, in words.

The kernel evaluates the exponential only on inputs shifted by the row maximum, using a fixed binary32 exponential that returns exactly 11 at 00 and +0+0 at every input at most −256-256; numerator and denominator are accumulated in binary32 and divided once; the quotient is cast once at the output boundary, to a fixed format that contains 00 and 11 exactly. The role of the threshold is arithmetic: since 256>150​ln⁡2256>150\ln 2, we have e−256<2−150e^{-256}<2^{-150}, the round-to-nearest midpoint between 00 and the least positive binary32 subnormal, so a correctly rounded binary32 exponential returns +0+0 on every input at most −256-256 (Appendix C).

Lemma 5.1 (softmax implements unique hardmax exactly).

Let (aj)j(a_{j})_{j} be a score row with unique maximizer j∗j^{*} and score gap at least 256256. Then the max-first kernel’s computed attention output is exactly vj∗v_{j^{*}}, independently of the row length, provided vj∗v_{j^{*}} is exactly representable in the accumulation format and preserved by the output cast—in particular for the values in {0,1}\{0,1\} used in this construction.

Proof.

By the kernel, the shifted inputs are a^j∗=0\hat{a}_{j^{*}}=0 and a^j≤−256\hat{a}_{j}\leq-256 for every j≠j∗j\neq j^{*}. The exponential row is exactly the one-hot indicator of j∗j^{*}: E32​(a^j∗)=1E_{32}(\hat{a}_{j^{*}})=1 and E32​(a^j)=+0E_{32}(\hat{a}_{j})=+0 for every j≠j∗j\neq j^{*}. Numerator and denominator are therefore the exact sums vj∗v_{j^{*}} and 11, each partial sum containing only zeros and one nonzero term. Division and the single boundary cast preserve the result. ∎

Corollary 5.2 (the main results hold under softmax).

Set Δ=256\Delta=256 in Section 4.2. Then every score row has scores in {256,0}\{256,0\}, a unique maximizer at distance wr−1w_{r}-1, and shifted losers exactly −256-256, all exactly representable in binary32. The value vectors are one-hot, and the remaining parameters and feed-forward computations use a fixed machine-dependent format as specified in Appendix B. By Lemma 5.1 every attention output equals the hardmax one-hot of Section 4.2 bit for bit, so Theorem 4.3 and Proposition 4.2 hold with softmax attention under the max-first kernel: the parameters are those of the hardmax construction rescaled by the fixed ratio between its score gap and the kernel constant 256256 (here 11, since Δ=256\Delta=256), the resources are unchanged, and the bit-size is still O⁡(1)O(1), independent of nn and LL.

Remark (scope).

The result is conditional on the stated kernel, in three ways. First, it requires a binary32 exponential that returns +0+0 below a fixed threshold, without a positive floor, logit soft-capping, or an additive ε\varepsilon in the normalizer; the exact contract is Appendix C. Second, the arithmetic is fixed-format: values not exactly representable in it (arbitrary real value vectors, for instance) are outside the exactness statement. Third, no claim is made about kernels beyond the contract: subtract-max is standard in production softmax implementations (Appendix C records examples), but that observation is context, not a conformance proof, and in particular online and fused attention kernels with their own epilogues are not thereby covered. Appendix C also treats two variants: a kernel that does not subtract the maximum (then Section 4.2 can set the winner’s score to 00 and every other score to −256-256), and a kernel with a positive scale, canonically 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_{k}} (then instantiate Δ=⌈256​dk⌉\Delta=\lceil 256\sqrt{d_{k}}\rceil; here dk=Kd_{k}=K is a machine constant, so Δ\Delta remains O⁡(1)O(1)). Nothing generalizes to exact-real softmax.

The comparison with exact-real arithmetic is a comparison of assumptions. Brösamle and Eckstein (2026) simulate Turing machines with low-precision softmax and summarized CoT, separating the winner from the other scores with depth, width, and precision that grow logarithmically. The present construction fixes a constant score gap and lets finite-format underflow make the selection exact; the only added cost is that constant gap Δ\Delta. These are different precision and architecture assumptions. We do not claim that their arithmetic implements exact hard selection.

6 Related work

We keep this section argument-driven; Appendix D carries the detailed comparison table of transformers simulating (t,s)(t,s)-bounded Turing machines, with per-row notes and normalized notation.

Transformer expressivity.

RASP models transformers as readable programs (Weiss et al., 2021; Lindner et al., 2023). Variants such as B-RASP, C-RASP, and RASP-L, together with subsequent formal-language analyses, characterize the languages recognized under different architectural restrictions (Angluin et al., 2024; Yang and Chiang, 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Strobl et al., 2024; Strobl et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025); see Strobl et al. (2024) for a survey. On the circuit side, Merrill and Sabharwal (2023) show that constant-depth, log-precision transformers without CoT are limited to 𝖳𝖢0\mathsf{TC}^{0}-style shallow circuits. Feng et al. (2023) connect CoT length to circuit depth: polynomially long CoT lifts transformers from shallow-circuit problems to all of 𝖯\mathsf{P}.

Looped transformers and latent thought.

Looped transformers extend serial computation by re-applying a shared block (Giannou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Geiping et al., 2025); Merrill and Sabharwal (2025) show that logarithmically deep looped transformers recognize regular languages and solve graph connectivity without CoT. Saunshi et al. (2025) study how latent thought can simulate computations expressed through CoT. Xu and Sato (2026) establish simulation results and complexity-class characterizations for CoT and latent thought, together with conditional separations: latent iterations support more efficient parallel computation in their deterministic setting, while stochastic CoT has advantages for approximate counting and sampling under their stated assumptions. Their deterministic comparison allows the embedding dimension to grow with input length. Our result is complementary: for a fixed Turing machine and hierarchy parameter, we construct a family with fixed machine-dependent learned size and precision in which varying LL exchanges explicit CoT steps for latent iterations. We account for generated tokens, visible context, serial loop work, and persistent per-iteration KV state under the loaded-cache interface. This is an interpolation for the constructed recurrent simulation, not an equivalence of arbitrary CoT and latent-thought models or a claim that all intermediate tokens can be eliminated.

Autoregressive Turing-machine simulations.

Autoregressive transformers are Turing-complete (Pérez et al., 2021; Bhattamishra et al., 2020; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024; Li et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025), with precisions and dimensions ranging from unbounded to constant. Jiang et al. (2026) establish softmax Turing completeness via counter machines with full-history attention and no fixed numerical-precision bound. Two later lines of work bring the context down to the space bound. Context-management schemes erase or summarize intermediate CoT: PENCIL (Yang et al., 2025) achieves maximal context O⁡(s⁡(n))O(s(n)), and Cui et al. (2026) show that the management policy itself determines the computable class; Brösamle and Eckstein (2026) keep every segment at O⁡(s⁡(n))O(s(n)) with low-precision softmax, at logarithmically growing depth, width, and precision. Sliding-window attention uses locality in place of erasure: Schuurmans et al. (2024) gave the earliest bounded-window universality, with a circular-queue context; Li and Wang (2025a) prove constant-bit-size Turing completeness for an O⁡(s⁡(n))O(s(n)) window via a Post-machine simulation and characterize 𝖶𝖨𝖭𝖣𝖮𝖶⁡[s⁡(n)]=𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡[s⁡(n)]\mathsf{WINDOW}[s(n)]=\mathsf{SPACE}[s(n)]; Li et al. (2026) remove the need for positional encodings; and Li and Wang (2025b) reach O⁡(s​(n)1/k)O(s(n)^{1/k}) CoT tokens per TM step, with window s⁡(n)+1s(n)+1, by increasing the head–layer product. Our construction starts from that last simulation and folds LL of its transitions into each token by making the queue representation layer-aligned (Section 4.5). At L=1L=1 it recovers that simulation’s bounds.

7 Discussion

The following limitations bound the result.

  • •

    Loaded cache. The input is pre-loaded into the initial KV cache (Section 4.3); the initialization cost is excluded from all bounds, and ordinary prompt prefill is not proved to produce the required entries.

  • •

    Visible resources only. The factor-LL reduction applies to generated tokens and to the visible window only; total cached KV state and serial block work are unchanged from L=1L=1.

  • •

    Kernel-conditional softmax. The softmax result holds only under the max-first binary32 contract of Appendix C, for values exactly representable in the accumulation and output formats; it does not extend to exact-real softmax, to kernels with positive floors or logit soft-capping, or to production kernels beyond that contract.

  • •

    Generated tokens are machine states. The visible trace is a sequence of internal machine-state symbols at stride LL, not a natural-language chain of thought; CoT-length statements concern this trace.

  • •

    No learning claims. Nothing here shows that such computations are learned by pretraining, reinforcement learning, or any other training signal; the messages of Section 1 are conjectural, and the supervision question for strided traces is open.

  • •

    Bounds, not measurements. All quantitative statements are asymptotic bounds of the construction; no experiment, speedup, or deployment claim is made.

Appendix A Congruent queue lengths

Grouping LL consecutive steps of a synchronous KK-queue machine into a single block requires that the front of queue rr at global step L​i+lLi+l be the symbol written at the same intra-block offset of an earlier block. That symbol was written at step L​i+l−ℓr+1Li+l-\ell_{r}+1, so the alignment

L​i+l−ℓr+1=L⁡(i−wr+1)+lLi+l-\ell_{r}+1\;=\;L(i-w_{r}+1)+l

holds for all ii and 0≤l<L0\leq l<L if and only if

ℓr≡1(modL),wr=ℓr−1L+1.\ell_{r}\equiv 1\pmod{L},\qquad w_{r}=\frac{\ell_{r}-1}{L}+1.

In the conversion of Fact 2.2, level gg has two content-half queues of length BgB^{g} and one buffer queue of length 2​Bg2B^{g}, where B=⌈s​(n)1/k⌉B=\lceil s(n)^{1/k}\rceil. We split the buffer into two queues of length BgB^{g}, so that all four physical queues per stack at the level have the same length.

Lemma A.1.

Prescribe L=L⁡(n)≥1L=L(n)\geq 1 and choose a fixed integer k≥1k\geq 1 satisfying s​(n)1/k=Ω⁡(L)s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L). Let B=⌈s​(n)1/k⌉B=\lceil s(n)^{1/k}\rceil and

b=min{b′≥max{B,L+1}:b′≡1(modL)},ℓg=bg(1≤g≤k).b=\min\bigl\{\,b^{\prime}\geq\max\{B,\ L+1\}\ :\ b^{\prime}\equiv 1\pmod{L}\,\bigr\},\qquad\ell_{g}=b^{\,g}\qquad(1\leq g\leq k).

Then the conversion can be implemented with K=8​k​k′K=8kk^{\prime} queues, all four queues per stack at level gg having length ℓg\ell_{g}. Every queue length satisfies ℓg≡1(modL)\ell_{g}\equiv 1\pmod{L}, and the resulting machine runs in O⁡(t⁡(n)​s​(n)1/k)O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}) steps using O⁡(k′​s​(n))O(k^{\prime}s(n)) queue space. Moreover,

wr=ℓr−1L+1≥2,w=O⁡(s⁡(n)L).w_{r}=\frac{\ell_{r}-1}{L}+1\geq 2,\qquad w=O\!\left(\frac{s(n)}{L}\right).
Proof.

Run the conversion of Fact 2.2 with geometric base bb. Replacing BB by b≥Bb\geq B preserves the divisibility between consecutive levels and provides at least the original capacity. Split each length-2​ℓg2\ell_{g} buffer, as any queue of length m1+m2m_{1}+m_{2} can be simulated step-for-step by two queues of lengths m1m_{1} and m2m_{2}; each stack now uses four length-ℓg\ell_{g} queues per level, so a k′k^{\prime}-tape machine uses 2⋅4​k​k′=8​k​k′2\cdot 4kk^{\prime}=8kk^{\prime} queues. The split simulation is step-for-step equivalent to the original one.

By minimality,

b≤max⁡{B,L+1}+L−1=O⁡(s​(n)1/k),b\leq\max\{B,L+1\}+L-1=O(s(n)^{1/k}),

because L=O⁡(s​(n)1/k)L=O(s(n)^{1/k}). Together with b≥Bb\geq B, this gives b=Θ⁡(s​(n)1/k)b=\Theta(s(n)^{1/k}) and ℓk=bk=Θ⁡(s⁡(n))\ell_{k}=b^{k}=\Theta(s(n)). The conversion therefore takes O⁡(t⁡(n)​b)=O⁡(t⁡(n)​s​(n)1/k)O(t(n)b)=O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}) steps and O⁡(k′​∑g=1kℓg)=O⁡(k′​s​(n))O(k^{\prime}\sum_{g=1}^{k}\ell_{g})=O(k^{\prime}s(n)) queue space. Finally, b≡1(modL)b\equiv 1\pmod{L} implies ℓg=bg≡1(modL)\ell_{g}=b^{g}\equiv 1\pmod{L}, while b≥L+1b\geq L+1 gives wr≥2w_{r}\geq 2; hence w=Θ⁡(ℓk/L)=O⁡(s⁡(n)/L)w=\Theta(\ell_{k}/L)=O(s(n)/L). ∎

The construction introduces no additional transitions, so τ⁡(n)=O⁡(t⁡(n)​s​(n)1/k)\tau(n)=O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}), the run length used in Proposition 4.2 and Theorem 4.3.

B.8 Faithfulness

Proposition B.1.

Under the initialization of Section 4.3, the transformer of B.1–B.7 emits, at each pass i≥w−1i\geq w-1, the token (qL⁡(i+1),σL⁡(i+1))(q_{L(i+1)},\sigma_{L(i+1)}), and after ⌈τ⁡(n)/L⌉\lceil\tau(n)/L\rceil passes the terminal token matching MM’s verdict on xx; there is no other behavior.

Proof.

The proof of Lemma 4.1 (Section 4.3) rests on two structural facts that hold verbatim for the components above: (a) within a pass, state moves only through the residual stream — the attention reads same-iteration value entries only, and each iteration’s feed-forward network consumes the fronts its attention wrote; (b) value entries are frozen at write time. With the base case supplied by the initialization of Section 4.3 and the retrieval identity of B.3, the two-stage induction of Section 4.3 goes through unchanged; the output head of B.6 turns the final residual into the token or the verdict, and the absorbing convention makes mid-pass halting consistent. ∎

Appendix C The exact softmax kernel contract

This appendix records the kernel contract of Section 5 exactly, the arithmetic behind the −256-256 threshold, and the two kernel variants. Every attention score is a finite binary32 value (IEEE single precision; RN32\mathrm{RN}_{32} denotes round-to-nearest in binary32). Given a score row (aj)j(a_{j})_{j} and value vectors (vj)j(v_{j})_{j}, the kernel computes the attention output as follows:

  • •

    (i) compute the row maximum μ=maxj⁡aj\mu=\max_{j}a_{j};

  • •

    (ii) form the shifted inputs a^j=RN32​(aj−μ)\hat{a}_{j}=\mathrm{RN}_{32}(a_{j}-\mu);

  • •

    (iii) apply a fixed binary32 exponential primitive E32E_{32} with E32​(0)=1E_{32}(0)=1 and E32​(x)=+0E_{32}(x)=+0 for every x≤−256x\leq-256;

  • •

    (iv) accumulate the numerator ∑jE32​(a^j)​vj\sum_{j}E_{32}(\hat{a}_{j})\,v_{j} and the normalizer ∑jE32​(a^j)\sum_{j}E_{32}(\hat{a}_{j}) in binary32, dividing only after both sums;

  • •

    (v) cast the quotient once, at the output boundary, to a fixed format containing 00 and 11 exactly.

The exactness of Lemma 5.1 additionally requires the winner’s value vj∗v_{j^{*}} to be exactly representable in the accumulation format and preserved by the boundary cast; the fixed format of (v) contains 00 and 11 exactly, which covers the one-hot values used in this construction (Corollary 5.2), and not arbitrary real value vectors.

The threshold.

Since 256>150​ln⁡2256>150\ln 2, we have e−256<2−150e^{-256}<2^{-150}, the round-to-nearest midpoint between 00 and the least positive binary32 subnormal 2−1492^{-149}, so a correctly rounded binary32 exponential returns +0+0 on every input at most −256-256. Flush-to-zero only strengthens the property. Any cutoff larger than 150​ln⁡2150\ln 2 in magnitude has the same property; 256=28256=2^{8} is chosen so that the rescaling factor of Corollary 5.2 is a power of two.

Remark.

(1) The lemma requires a binary32 exponential that returns +0+0 below a fixed threshold, without positive floor or logit soft-capping. (2) Subtracting the maximum converts overflow into underflow and thereby helps to simulate hard selection. We include it in our softmax kernel because it is standard in production implementations.11 1 PyTorch’s CPU and CUDA softmax kernels (host_softmax and SoftMax.cu’s epilogue exp⁡(input−max)/sum\exp(\mathrm{input}-\mathrm{max})/\mathrm{sum}), FlashAttention’s online softmax (exponentiating score⋅scale−max⋅scale\mathrm{score}\cdot\mathrm{scale}-\mathrm{max}\cdot\mathrm{scale}), Triton’s fused-softmax kernel (“subtract maximum for numerical stability”), and TensorFlow’s softmax op (shifted_logits = logits - max) all evaluate the exponential only on inputs shifted by the row maximum. This observation concerns that one step; it does not establish full conformance of any production kernel, in particular not of online or fused implementations with their own epilogues. For a kernel that does not subtract the maximum, the positional encoding of Section 4.2 can set the winner’s score to 00 and every other score to −256-256. (3) If the kernel includes a positive scale, canonically 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_{k}}, instantiate Δ=⌈256​dk⌉\Delta=\lceil 256\sqrt{d_{k}}\rceil. Here dk=Kd_{k}=K is a machine constant, so Δ\Delta remains O⁡(1)O(1).
